Let's dive into the fascinating world of coral reefs, which provide crucial habitat for a wide variety of fish and other marine organisms.
The reefs themselves are created by countless tiny creatures known as coral polyps.
Each polyp is a small, soft-bodied animal that lives in colonies and secretes calcium carbonate.
This calcium carbonate then forms the hard skeletons that build up coral reefs over time.
What's truly remarkable is that coral polyps contain microscopic organisms, called algae, inside the coral's own tissues.
These algae transform sunlight into usable energy by performing the process of photosynthesis.
This way, the algae provide the coral polyps with most of their energy.
So the algae and corals are in a mutually beneficial relationship that fuels the entire reef ecosystem.
But coral reefs are in trouble.
One of the most pressing threats they face is coral bleaching.
When ocean temperatures rise, as they do today, coral polyps often become stressed and expel the algae living in their tissues.
This not only turns the corals ghostly white but also strips them of their main energy source.
If the stress continues, the polyps can die, leaving behind a lifeless reef structure and threatening the entire ecosystem that depends on it.
Scientists are bringing some coral reefs back to life through a method called coral gardening.
Scientists grow healthy coral fragments in underwater nurseries and transplant them to degraded reefs.
This hands-on restoration technique helps rebuild reef structures, support marine life, and even select heat-resistant coral strains for future resilience.
